text:
**Short answer: yes at about $449 or less, if you mainly run AC appliances. If you can find a newer model at a similar price, it's probably the better buy.**

**What's good**
- **Real capacity:** Testers got 82-90% of the rated 1,152 Wh, roughly 950-1,030 Wh ([Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/), [PCWorld](https://www.pcworld.com/article/1966571/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review.html)).
- **Power and battery:** It has 1,800 W continuous output, and a LiFePO4 battery rated for 3,500+ cycles with a 5-year warranty ([BLUETTI US](https://www.bluettipower.com/products/ac180?variant=44099774480603)).
- **Charging:** It charges fast, about 1.3 hours from empty in OutdoorGearLab's testing ([OutdoorGearLab](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/reviews/camping-and-hiking/power-station/bluetti-ac180)).
- **Value:** Its cost per usable Wh is among the lowest of the models Watt Power Station tracks.

**What's not**
- **Weight:** At about 36 lb it's heavy for its capacity. OutdoorGearLab scored it 66 overall and noted a noisy fan.
- **Small loads:** Efficiency drops a lot on light loads. Outdoor Life measured only 54% of rated capacity at about 34 W, which matters for a CPAP or an overnight fridge ([Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)).
- **DC efficiency:** PCWorld measured only 71% on a USB-style DC load ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/)).
- **Expansion:** Bluetti's marketing implies expansion, but it isn't truly expandable. It can only be topped up from a B80/B230/B300 battery in Power Bank Mode ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac180)).
- **Power Lifting:** The 2,700 W mode only works for resistive heating loads, and not while charging from the wall.
- **Heat and UPS:** Output drops to 1,500 W above 95 °F. For UPS use, the "Grid Enhancement" app setting must be off or backup can fail ([Best Batteries](https://us.best-batteries.com/reviews/bluetti-ac180/)).
- **Possibly discontinued:** Some listings show limited stock or discontinuation signals, so confirm the exact variant before ordering.

**Price and where to buy**
- Bluetti's store lists it at $499 ([BLUETTI AC180](https://www.bluettipower.com/products/ac180?variant=44099774480603)).
- Dealectric says code AFF5OFF takes $24.95 off, and that's an affiliate link ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac180)).
- An Amazon listing was $449 on Oct 24 ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/)). Check that it's the standalone unit and not a bundle.

**Alternatives to compare**
OutdoorGearLab says the successor, the **BLUETTI Elite 100 V2**, is smaller, lighter (25 lb), quieter and charges faster, with slightly less capacity (1,024 Wh). It also recommends the **Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2** as a better choice that costs less. Watt Power Station lists them at about $489 and $499.99 ([comparison](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)). I didn't get direct purchase links for those two.

**Bottom line:** For occasional camping or outages with AC loads, the AC180 at $449 or under is solid. If you'll carry it often, run small loads overnight, or can get the Elite 100 V2 or Anker for about the same money, go with one of those.
